passage_text: Researchers investigated the effects of different cognitive training protocols on reaction time in a controlled laboratory setting. A total of 120 participants, aged 18-35, were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group that received no training, and three experimental groups that received distinct training regimens (A, B, and C). Each training protocol consisted of 30 minutes of computer-based exercises over five consecutive days. Reaction time was measured using a standardized computerized task before the first training session and immediately after the final session. The results, summarized in Table 1, indicate that all experimental groups exhibited reductions in mean reaction time relative to the control group. Group B showed the largest mean reduction, followed by Groups C and A. Standard deviations varied modestly across groups, suggesting comparable variability in performance. These findings suggest that specific training protocols may differentially enhance cognitive processing speed, with potential implications for occupational performance and clinical rehabilitation. Future studies should examine long-term retention and transfer effects to real-world tasks.
table_data:
Group | Mean Response Time (ms) | Standard Deviation (ms)
Control | 650 | 45
Treatment A | 590 | 48
Treatment B | 530 | 50
Treatment C | 560 | 47
stem: Which group had the lowest mean reaction time after training?
explanation: Treatment B’s mean reaction time (530 ms) is lower than the other groups.
trap: Choosing Control because it received no training, or misreading the table; the lowest mean (530 ms) belongs to Treatment B.

stem: Which experimental design would best test whether Treatment B improves reaction time compared to Control?
explanation: A randomized controlled trial with blinding controls for bias and establishes causality.
trap: Choosing an observational or survey design: these cannot separate the effect of Treatment B from differences between the people who chose or received it.

stem: Which of the following statements is false regarding the data?

options.A: All groups had similar standard deviations.
options.B: Treatment B had the greatest mean reduction.
options.C: Treatment A had the highest mean reaction time after training.
options.D: Control group had the highest mean reaction time.

explanation: Control (650 ms) had the highest mean; Treatment A (590 ms) was not the highest.
trap: Treating Treatment A as the group with the highest post-training RT; Control, which had no training, had the highest (650 ms) versus 590 ms for A.

stem: Which of the following best links the results to a potential application in occupational performance?

options.A: The findings suggest training protocols could improve reaction time for high‑speed tasks like air traffic control.
options.B: The data indicate that no training improves reaction time.
options.C: The results show that reaction time is unrelated to cognitive processing speed.
options.D: The study proves that all training regimens are equally effective.

explanation: Improved reaction time is directly relevant to high‑speed occupational tasks such as air traffic control.
trap: Choosing the option claiming no benefit or equal effects, which contradicts the table (590, 530, 560 ms versus 650 ms for Control).
